audience.programmeDescription: Students study religious traditions, texts and practices alongside social questions. They draw on anthropology, sociology and philosophy to investigate power, migration, media and cultural change.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR combination examines religious belief and practice through myth, religious art, material heritage, freedom of religion and the politics of identity. Radboud teaches a wider range of religious traditions in depth and applies religious studies to care and climate.

curriculum.routeLabel: Ordinary full-time bachelor; Religion and Care plus Worldviews, Nature and Climate modules
curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC framework includes 120 EC of required study, two complete 15 EC modules and 30 EC of free choice. Each selected module has three 5 EC courses. Research includes a supervised project and a 10 EC individual final work. RADAr-NL carries no credits; an equivalent university test can support exemption. The usual first-year study-advice threshold is 44 EC. External electives and internships need applicable approval; professional careers may require further qualifications.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives.
Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims.
Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law.
Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self.
Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading.
Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy.
Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers.
Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns.
Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives.
Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline.
Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination.
Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory.
Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations.
Examines youth radicalization and educational prevention through psychology, education, sociology, political science and peace education.
Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa.
Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings.
This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world.
Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception.
Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis.
This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present.
Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization.
Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty.
Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture.
